name: Primrose Yellow
lede: Primrose yellow is a pale, slightly greenish yellow named for the wild primrose; naturalists fixed it in the early 1800s, and paint makers later gave the same name to several unrelated pale chromate pigments.

sections.title: A flower, a canary and a lump of sulphur
sections.body:
Primrose yellow entered the naturalists' vocabulary through Werner's color nomenclature as English-edited by Patrick Syme [1]. In Syme's 1814 edition it is number 63 in the yellows, and each color is pinned to three examples: the pale canary bird among animals, the wild primrose among plants, and pale-colored sulphur among minerals [1]. Baty credits Syme with introducing the term to naturalists in 1814, along with violet purple, China blue and gallstone yellow [2].

The same book gives a recipe: gamboge yellow mixed with a little sulphur yellow and a great deal of snow white [1]. That makes the color a tint, a yellow thinned with white, which is why it reads as pale and soft rather than as a strong hue. In the same system, sienna yellow is built from primrose yellow plus a little ochre yellow, so the colors form a chain of small steps [3].

The name stayed in use. Cleaveland's 1816 mineralogy lists primrose yellow among its eighty colors, between sulphur yellow and wax yellow [4]. Ridgway kept it in his 1912 color standards, which, by Baty's count, took over at least 19 of Syme's terms [5]. Our library has it from three sources: Werner, Ridgway's plate XXX, and ISCC-NBS block 101, and the Maerz and Paul dictionary dates the name to 1629 [6]. That is earlier than Syme, so the English name is older than the naturalists' fixing of it [2][6]. The books we hold do not say who first used it.

sections.title: Which primrose is on the screen
sections.body:
The swatch on this page is the color our library lists for Primrose Yellow, #EBDD99, a light, muted yellow [6]. Ridgway's own plate reads very slightly differently, as a scan of an aged plate, so any screen version is approximate [6]. The nearest named neighbors in our data are soft beiges, which is what a pale yellow with some grey in it turns into [6].

A real primrose petal is a little paler and a little greener than many people expect. The naturalists' example is the wild primrose, *Primula vulgaris*, and Syme's recipe is tuned to it: mostly white, a touch of green-leaning sulphur yellow [1]. If you want to learn the color, look at an old primrose in shade, not at a daffodil.

sections.title: The paint called primrose
sections.body:
Paint makers took the name for pale yellows made from chromates, and the chemistry behind it changes from one source to the next. Ball explains the first route: lead chromate can be made with an admixed lead sulphate, and half and half of the two salts gives a primrose yellow, while a mixture richer in chromate, 65 per cent, is a lemon yellow, and more chromate deepens the tone further [7]. In the Pigment Compendium, chrome primrose and primrose chrome were still current terms in 1928, meaning a very pale tint of lead chromate, or chromate and sulphate of lead [8].

A second meaning appears in the same reference. A Winsor and Newton catalogue of 1896 lists primrose yellow as chromates of zinc and barium, and Heaton in 1928 defines it as zinc chrome [8]. So the same label was applied to a lead pigment and to a zinc pigment, and a painter who bought a tube by the name could not know which one was in it from the name alone [8].

A third meaning is modern. In 1976 Du Pont described a brilliant primrose yellow made from bismuth vanadate, a compound first reported in 1924 and developed into pigments only from the mid-1970s [9]. All three are pale clean yellows, but they are different substances. The color name followed the look, not the chemistry.

sections.title: Where to look in painting
sections.body:
Primrose yellow is a light color, and in paintings it works as one. In our archive it plays a light in about 60 per cent of the 277 paintings where it appears inside the picture, judged by lightness rank within each painting, so that varnish cannot fake the result [10]. Painters use it for cloth, sky glow and highlights more than for anything dark.

The best way to train the eye is to compare it with its neighbors. [[lemon-yellow]] is sharper and more saturated, [[sulphur-yellow]] greener, [[straw]] a little browner, and [[cream]] more white [6]. Primrose sits between them: the yellow you notice only because the white around it is slightly colder.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, the color appears in 472 paintings by area (about 1.98 per cent) and in 277 by the within-painting lens, as photographed [10]. That makes it more common than 76 per cent of the named colors [10]. It peaks in the 1900s, when 27 of the 1,674 paintings we hold from that century carry it, which is 1.6 times the museums' baseline [10].

The earliest match in the archive is 1305, but the early centuries are thin and the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of any pigment or dye [10]. Jan Maurits Quinkhard has it in 4 of 40 works here, the highest share of any painter, though no painter stands out against the baseline [10]. In printed English the word *primrose* peaks around 1885, as the Ngram data relative to its peak shows, and this counts the flower and the place names too, not only the color [10]. Every number here is a look-alike count and not a pigment test [10].

openers: Primrose yellow is a recipe: a little gamboge, a touch of sulphur yellow, and mostly snow white.
Paint called primrose has been lead chromate, zinc and barium chromate, and bismuth vanadate, depending on the decade.
